sys.path.append(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))

from exllamav3 import Config, Model, Cache, Tokenizer, Generator, Job
from PIL import Image
from common import format_prompt, get_stop_conditions
import requests
import torch
torch.set_printoptions(precision = 5, sci_mode = False, linewidth=200)

mode = "gemma3"
cache_size = 8192
streaming = True

if mode == "gemma3":
    prompt_format = "gemma"
    model_dir = "/mnt/str/models/gemma3-4b-it/exl3/5.0bpw/"

images = [
    # Cat
    {"file": "media/cat.png"},

    # Line drawing
    # {"file": "media/strawberry.png"},

    # Random photo from picsum
    # {"url": "https://picsum.photos/800/600"},

    # Unrandom photo from picsum
    # {"url": "https://fastly.picsum.photos/id/451/800/600.jpg?hmac=B0-st7nsgJ0F8ufKM5HjVwP-1y_vIL60R-PpNFLITiQ"}
]

system_prompt = "You are a very nice language model."
instruction = "Describe the image."

def get_image(file = None, url = None):
    assert (file or url) and not (file and url)
    if file:
        script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
        file_path = os.path.join(script_dir, file)
        return Image.open(file_path)
    elif url:
        return Image.open(requests.get(url, stream = True).raw)

def main():

    # Load model with cache
    config = Config.from_directory(model_dir)
    model = Model.from_config(config)
    cache = Cache(model, max_num_tokens = cache_size)
    model.load(progressbar = True)
    tokenizer = Tokenizer.from_config(config)

    # Load the image component model
    vision_model = Model.from_config(config, component = "vision")
    vision_model.load(progressbar = True)

    # Create generator
    generator = Generator(
        model = model,
        cache = cache,
        tokenizer = tokenizer,
    )

    # Process images
    image_embeddings = [
        vision_model.get_image_embeddings(tokenizer = tokenizer, image = get_image(**img_args))
        for img_args in images
    ]

    # Build string of placeholder symbols that will be tokenized as image embeddings
    placeholders = "\n".join([ie.text_alias for ie in image_embeddings]) + "\n"

    # Format prompt
    prompt = format_prompt(prompt_format, system_prompt, placeholders + instruction)

    # Streaming response
    if streaming:
        input_ids = tokenizer.encode(
            prompt,
            encode_special_tokens = True,
            embeddings = image_embeddings,
        )

        job = Job(
            input_ids = input_ids,
            max_new_tokens = 500,
            decode_special_tokens = True,
            stop_conditions = get_stop_conditions(prompt_format, tokenizer),
            embeddings = image_embeddings,
        )

        generator.enqueue(job)

        print()
        print(prompt, end = "", flush = True)
        while generator.num_remaining_jobs():
            results = generator.iterate()
            for result in results:
                text = result.get("text", "")
                print(text, end = "", flush = True)
        print()

    # Non-streaming
    else:
        output = generator.generate(
            prompt = prompt,
            max_new_tokens = 500,
            encode_special_tokens = True,
            decode_special_tokens = True,
            stop_conditions = get_stop_conditions(prompt_format, tokenizer),
            embeddings = image_embeddings,
        )
        print(output)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()", "encoding": "utf-8", "mode": "100644"}}

{"ok": true, "result": {"offset": 0, "next_offset": 7080, "truncated": false, "text": "{
  "discussion": {
    "author_login": "Downtown-Case",
    "created_at": "2025-04-28T21:11:52Z",
    "kind": "issue",
    "number": 29,
    "state": "OPEN",
    "title": "Auto-YaRN for Qwen3? Maybe even set it dynamically?",
    "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/29"
  },
  "objects": [
    {
      "author_login": "Downtown-Case",
      "content": "It appears Qwen3 is using YaRN for long contexts, like Qwen 2.5:\n\n> The maximum context length in pre-training for Qwen3 models is 32,768 tokens. It can be extended to 131,072 tokens with RoPE scaling techniques. We have validated the performance with YaRN.\n\nhttps://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3/blob/main/docs/source/inference/transformers.md#enabling-long-context\n\nEditing the config file for the desired context is... less than ideal for users.\n\n*However*, they mention this little nugget:\n\n> Transformers implements static YaRN, which means the scaling factor remains constant regardless of input length, potentially impacting performance on shorter texts. We advise adding the rope_scaling configuration only when processing long contexts is required. It is also recommended to modify the factor as needed. For example, if the typical context length for your application is 65,536 tokens, it would be better to set factor as 2.0\n\nThe default factor is 4.0, and currently the exllama code will stick to that if the 'default' long context configuration is present: https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/blob/0ff9fd2e39f6307e54358fd1a48a50b5cf7307f8/exllamav3/util/rope.py#L130-L159\n\nBut it *appears* a more optimal thing to do is ignore the rope_scaling factor, and statically set it with `(context length of the loaded model)/original_max_position_embeddings`, which would be 2.0 for 64K, 3.0 for 96K, and so on.\n\nThis is trivially easy to implement, but the question is if exllamav3 should set it automatically like that. *I say* it should, as most users aren't going to dig into how YaRN scaling works and match the scaling factor to their specified context length. \n\n***\n\n...But what would be *even more optimal* would be to dynamically set the scaling factor per request. For instance, if a 64K request was recieved, set it to 2.0. A 96K one, 3.0. So each request gets the optimal factor.\n\nEven better would be to disable YaRN entirely for requests under 32K.\n\n...Is this practical to do? I seem to remember it not being practical in exllamav2.",
      "content_sha256": "f505041ef1da166271f0762661d69c5411ca9f4f65a242fc03bb0c98533e4aec",
      "created_at": "2025-04-28T21:11:52Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-04-28T21:22:59Z",
      "source_id": "I_kwDOOU24Gs60YMCp",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/29"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "The RoPE parameters has an override that could be used at load time, though it's currently only used for longrope:\n\n```py\n@dataclass\nclass RopeSettings:\n    head_dim: int = 128\n    rope_theta: float = 10000.0\n    rope_scaling: dict | None = None\n    partial_rotary_factor: float = 1.0\n    max_position_embeddings: int | None = None\n    original_max_position_embeddings: int | None = None\n    rope_style: RopeStyle = RopeStyle.NEOX\n    override_max_position_embeddings: int | None = None\n```\n\nIt's a total nightmare to deal with, though, honestly. Changing the scaling factor dynamically breaks just about every assumption made in the generator, and I'm not sure how to even approach stuff like a new set of frequencies per request, since the generator can batch together sequences of different length. It can also reuse cached values from a previous sequence, and that would have to go as well if position IDs have to be reinterpreted based on the overall max sequence length.",
      "content_sha256": "a08fda8a21287e64e3e9545ea558c0ed1535f11e2605a000427bb88570fc74a8",
      "created_at": "2025-04-29T17:48:03Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-04-29T17:48:03Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6pQrEb",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/29#issuecomment-2839720219"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "Downtown-Case",
      "content": "Ah, yeah, it's *not* worth breaking anything. Forget per-request dynamism. It doesn't seem that great past 32K it in my few API tests anyway.\n\nHow about a log warning? Maybe a print statement along the lines of \"WARNING: A scaling factor of 2.0 is recommended for a context size of 65536!\"\n\n\n\n",
      "content_sha256": "0456aba3feb9fb20ead84c81df8e53f8b5b7d377d957c0af9e9d60951fca30df",
      "created_at": "2025-04-29T18:29:42Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-04-29T18:30:24Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6pRKjT",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/29#issuecomment-2839849171"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "Downtown-Case",
      "content": "An interesting datapoint: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-32B/discussions/18\n\nTL;DR: Qwen3 32B 3.45bpw, squeezed into 24GB, got a math/reasoning question from a 107K prompt! Exllamav2/Qwen2.5 (with YaRN) wasn't even close to that in my testing, though admittedly I never tested QwQ like that.\n\nIn other words, YaRN is surprisingly effective with Qwen3, and setting the correct scaling factor seems to be important.",
      "content_sha256": "2cd7a40099c3908ed8d92a792207b99b6126ad5dd87ef4fffdf18792fde13b40",
      "created_at": "2025-04-30T14:19:09Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-04-30T14:21:41Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6pZ7hi",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/29#issuecomment-2842146914"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "Lissanro",
      "content": "I am interested in this as well, so decided to share my thoughts below in case they are useful.\n\n> what would be even more optimal would be to dynamically set the scaling factor per request. For instance, if a 64K request was recieved, set it to 2.0. A 96K one, 3.0. So each request gets the optimal factor.\n\nI think request length does not include reply that will be generated, so setting it dynamically would need setting it after every generated token (but please correct me if I misunderstand how YaRN supposed to work with growing context while the model generates reply for the given request).\n\n>  ignore the rope_scaling factor, and statically set it with (context length of the loaded model)/original_max_position_embeddings\n\nI like this idea, but if it will be considered for an implementation and enabled by default, I suggest adding command-line option that allows to disable it if needed.",
      "content_sha256": "ce8de507c8ea893dad30beeeacf1ef899d5a272cbddef04eed546d589df5a23d",
      "created_at": "2025-05-01T02:15:46Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-05-01T02:17:40Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6pgus5",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/29#issuecomment-2843929401"
    }
  ]
}

{"ok": true, "result": {"offset": 0, "next_offset": 16000, "truncated": true, "text": "{
  "discussion": {
    "author_login": "louiehelm",
    "created_at": "2025-04-28T03:39:01Z",
    "kind": "pull_request",
    "number": 26,
    "state": "OPEN",
    "title": "Superior 3INST parameters",
    "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/pull/26"
  },
  "objects": [
    {
      "author_login": "louiehelm",
      "content": "Summary: Swapped out original LCG params in 3INST for a better, computationally screened, optimal MCG multiplier\r\n\r\n0.2-3.9% lower PPL\r\n1.25% faster processing (addition removed)\r\n\r\n\r\nDetails:\r\n\r\n3INST's default LCG params are knowably suboptimal:\r\nx = 89226354 * x + 64248484\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\n| Property | 89,226,354 (0x5517C72) | 4,286,219,237 (0xFF7A83E5) |\r\n|----------|-------------------|----------------------|\r\n| Odd | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| >sqrt(2^32) | \u2705 | \u2705 |\r\n| >2^32/2 = 2147483648 | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| Congruent 5 (mod 8) | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| High figure of merit | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| \"Spectrally good\" in higher dimensions | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| Maximum potency | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n\r\n\r\nSee [Computationally easy, spectrally good multipliers for congruential pseudorandom number generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.05304) for deeper discussion\r\n\r\nDemanding LCGs have good spectral properties is not always necessary but for a 256-diminsion Trellis Decoder, spectral quality in higher dimensions is actually a key performance requirement.\r\n\r\nScreened all 45458 spectrally good LCG multipliers and all 49507 spectrally good MCG multipliers [uploaded to github](https://github.com/vigna/CPRNG) by @vigna\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nMany LCG multipliers had strictly lower RMS in the decoder but none had universally superior PPL when actually quantizing and decoding real models.\r\n\r\nBut several MCG multipliers had both lower RMS in a vacuum AND universally better PPL on several models @ multiple bitrates. The best one appears to be 0xFF7A83E5.\r\n\r\n![0xff7a83e5_codebook](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6d36f1e7-f4f1-4ce4-9407-155faba0f328)\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\n### Performance Comparison of Multiplier 0xFF7A83E5 Across Models\r\n\r\n| **Metric** | **Mistral-7B-instruct** | **Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct** |\r\n|------------|-------------------------|---------------------------|\r\n| **Original Baseline (89226354)** |  |  |\r\n| Baseline PPL@2.00 | 6.897755 | 23.382405 |\r\n| Baseline PPL@3.00 | 5.962067 | 15.637272 |\r\n| Baseline PPL@4.00 | 5.821786 | 14.540853 |\r\n| **With Multiplier 0xFF7A83E5** |  |  |\r\n| PPL@2.00 | 6.881336 | 22.464554 |\r\n| PPL@3.00 | 5.957563 | 15.410229 |\r\n| PPL@4.00 | 5.820617 | 14.468759 |\r\n| **Improvement (%)** |  |  |\r\n| Imp@2.00 | 0.238% | 3.93% |\r\n| Imp@3.00 | 0.076% | 1.45% |\r\n| Imp@4.00 | 0.020% | 0.50% |\r\n| **Overall Performance** |  |  |\r\n| Avg Improvement | 0.111% | 1.96% |\r\n| Total Improvement | 0.334% | 5.87% |\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nAlso inspected how this impacts the CUDA (removing addition):\r\n\r\nOriginal CUDA PTX:\r\nmad.lo.s32 \t%r4, %r3, -1997118179, 64248484;\r\nand.b32  \t%r5, %r4, -1879076865;\r\nxor.b32  \t%r2, %r5, 996162400;\r\n\r\nNew CUDA PTX:\r\nmul.lo.s32 \t%r4, %r3, -8748059;\r\nand.b32  \t%r5, %r4, -1879076865;\r\nxor.b32  \t%r2, %r5, 996162400;\r\n\r\n\r\nBenchmarking reveals small but measurable 1.25% speed increase by eliminating addition.\r\n\r\nEven modest 1.25% speedup and a small 0.2-3.9% lower PPL is hard to come by in other places, given how efficient EXL3 is shaping up to be.",
      "content_sha256": "0dfc2cdbb2ca372aca15de16d2812174f642375ca2491b88ba3e8b98f706fa09",
      "created_at": "2025-04-28T03:39:01Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-04-28T03:43:44Z",
      "source_id": "PR_kwDOOU24Gs6UGOU7",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/pull/26"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "This is very interesting. I will have to do a lot of tests, also on larger models, just to thoroughly verify this. Because to actually include it would require doubling the number of kernel instances and adding some metadata to quantized models to identify the new codebook (a bit too far along to just invalidate all existing EXL3 models.)\r\n\r\nI'm surprised there's a performance difference, but it looks like the compiler does produce an extra MOV instruction in the first case since 64248484 is more than 20 bits, and the GEMM kernel is currently running into an ALU bottleneck due to the trellis unpacking overhead (on Ampere mostly).\r\n\r\nAlso, was the 1.25% speed increase just the kernel latency or inference overall, and what hardware did you see this on?",
      "content_sha256": "4a0b6780f1256eb84b3335bea7001f8949481820d41a55e890954642b6d10af8",
      "created_at": "2025-04-28T12:54:28Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-04-28T12:54:28Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6o_PW9",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/pull/26#issuecomment-2835150269"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "louiehelm",
      "content": "More testing today with larger model:\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\n| **Metric** | **Llama 3.1 8B Instruct** | **Llama 3.1 70B Instruct** |\r\n|------------|--------------|--------------------------------|\r\n| **Original Baseline** |  |  |\r\n| Baseline PPL@2.00 | 10.421164 | 6.533785 |\r\n| Baseline PPL@3.00 | 8.119616 | 4.450084 |\r\n| Baseline PPL@4.00 | 7.756961 | 3.822873 |\r\n| **With Multiplier 0xff7a83e5** |  |  |\r\n| PPL@2.00 | 10.453533 | 6.543885 |\r\n| PPL@3.00 | 8.123410 | 4.422189 |\r\n| PPL@4.00 | 7.754818 | 3.835484 |\r\n| **Improvement (%)** |  |  |\r\n| Imp@2.00 | -0.31% | -0.15% |\r\n| Imp@3.00 | -0.05% | 0.63% |\r\n| Imp@4.00 | 0.03% | -0.33% |\r\n| **Overall Performance** |  |  |\r\n| Avg Improvement | -0.11% | 0.05% |\r\n| Total Improvement | -0.33% | 0.15% |\r\n\r\n\r\nFew minor regressions. Mostly breakeven. Biggest gain on 3.0bpw which already appears to be the format's new sweet spot.\r\n\r\n\r\nImproved parameter is most valuable if:\r\n1. Decoder improvement gives more measurable speedup on older hardware\r\n2. PPL improvements are more numerous and larger than minor regressions\r\n3. Other performance benchmarks bear out higher fidelity\r\n4. There's abstract benefit to having a principled parameter\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nHappy to run further evals. Which ones would be most helpful? Is there a KLD eval? Or another automated benchmark you find correlates well with actual model quality?\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\n> was the 1.25% speed increase just the kernel latency or inference overall\r\n\r\nJust the decoder's isolated CUDA routines in a vacuum.\r\n\r\n\r\n> and what hardware did you see this on?\r\n\r\n2 x 5090. Perhaps older hardware has larger speedup from improving the decoder?\r\n",
      "content_sha256": "407158efa717de79eed8aece1792ede65631a9727cbfa932a0d6118d8b3d2254",
      "created_at": "2025-04-29T16:11:05Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-04-29T16:11:05Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6pPv-2",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/pull/26#issuecomment-2839478198"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "Cutting out a MOV instruction is definitely worth it, even if it ends up breaking even on accuracy. I think if the difference is this small on perplexity, most likely it will be hard to detect any other way. I didn't write up a KLD test yet, but eval/model_diff.py would be a good place to start.\r\n\r\nI'm a little tied up with Qwen3 at the moment, but I will get back to working out a nice way to incorporate this.",
      "content_sha256": "b0dde3a2efca8a6ef13243008385e093f72cc5a236143bb198e539a8b45f5c29",
      "created_at": "2025-04-29T17:37:53Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-04-29T17:37:53Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6pQlxF",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/pull/26#issuecomment-2839698501"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "louiehelm",
      "content": "More evidence for 0xFF7A83E5\r\n--\r\nOut of curiosity, I coded my own routines to reproduce the QTIP paper's distortion rate calculations.\r\n\r\nGot slightly different results than what they reported:\r\n\r\n|                   | **My tests** | **QTIP** | **Difference** |\r\n|-------------------|--------------|----------|----------------|\r\n| LLOYD-MAX         | 0.1172       | 0.118    | 0.7%           |\r\n| 1MAD              | 0.0687       | 0.069    | 0.4%           |\r\n| DR(infinite)      | 0.0625       | 0.063    | 0.8%           |\r\n| 3INST             | 0.0743       | 0.069    | 7.7%           |\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nFirst 3 are nitpicks... essentially just replicating their work with 1 more sig fig.\r\n\r\n* Although, I'll note others have also published 0.0117 as the distortion rate for 2-bit Lloyd-Max\r\n* DR (infinite) = 2^(-2 * bitrate) = 2^(-2 * 2) = 2^-4 = 0.0625. Rounding to 0.063 feels odd for a tight theoretical lowerbound that only required one more digit to express precisely.\r\n* 1MAD is tiny bit below 0.069 at ~0.0687. This algorithm seems to have inherently more sample variance so 0.069 may be the best estimate -- and perhaps why they chose to report 2 sig figs across the board.\r\n\r\nHowever 3INST is more confusing:\r\n\r\n* 3INST: 0.0743 average distortion rate. Never collected a sample outside [0.072 - 0.076]\r\n\r\nTheir code shows they tested another decoder called 2MAD. My guess is 2MAD has a measured distortion rate of 0.069 too and they were initially planning to report both 1MAD and 2MAD results.  But then they found 3INST and probably decided that since 2MAD was just slower without being measurably better, they would instead only report 1MAD and 3INST data. But then somehow the data for 3INST distortion rate never got updated in Table 1 of the paper.\r\n\r\n\r\nIn any case, I've sampled the richest chunk of the MCG multiplier space and using abstract MSE measurements (rather than full end-to-end model quantizing / perplexity measures), 0xFF7A83E5 once again ranks at the top with the lowest avg distortion rate.\r\n\r\n3INST (MCG-0xFF7A83E5): 0.0726  (0.0017 lower distortion rate than original 3INST params)\r\n\r\nNext 3 best 3INST MCG multipliers:\r\n* 0xEAB209FD 0.001425\r\n* 0xFC275E4D 0.001256\r\n* 0xF2BAA58D 0.001239\r\n\r\n\r\nSo far only tested ~10% of the spectrally good MCG multipliers from Vigna's work for MSE improvements. Should complete exhaustive rankings in next couple days.\r\n\r\nBut it's good seeing a totally different evaluation criteria that uses completely separate code also identify the same exact multiplier as the best one.\r\n\r\nAnd relative to the original 3INST baseline, this multiplier produces 2.3% lower distortion which is roughly the average improvement I'm seeing in 2-bit model perplexity too. So this is a good sanity check that this particular parameter isn't just \"getting lucky\" on the specific models I've tested, but actually would be expected to be 2.3% better at 2-bits.\r\n\r\nMSE distortion rate at k=1 bit, 3 bits, 4 bits, and 5 bits all improved as well at roughly 3.3%, 2.0%, 1.6%, and 1.2% vs baselines.\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nLOP3 not currently used?\r\n--\r\n\r\nQTIP paper mentions how 3INST is especially good precisely because mask and xor step can be combined into one low level lop3 instruction.\r\n\r\nSo theoretically nvcc should render these two lines:\r\n\r\nx &= 0b10001111111111111000111111111111u;\r\nx ^= 0b00111011011000000011101101100000u;\r\n\r\nDown into something like this PTX instruction:\r\n\r\nasm(\"lop3.b32 %0, %1, 0x8FFF8FFF, 0x3B603B60, 0x6A;\" : \"=r\"(x) : \"r\"(x));\r\n\r\n\r\nBut nvcc never does this (at least on my system with sm120). Maybe it's not kosher to pass in the same register for an input and output with lop3? If so, changing CUDA code from \"x ^= ...\". into \"y = x ^ ...\" might be enough to fix this and help the compiler successfully find this optimization. I haven't found a painless way to reliably implement LOP3 yet but it's probably a trivial patch for a smart CUDA wizard. We have any of those around here? If LOP3 isn't getting implemented in any of the EXL3 decoder kernels and it's using 2 separate [and (...) and xor(...)] instruction every pass, that's another 8-10% speedup being left on the table. Maybe this will finally make Ampere perform better?\r\n\r\n\r\nThere might also be another clever way to shave off a mov in the final re-packing steps by ordering it slightly differently as well. But we can explore that later. It's the highest hanging fruit and can be optimized down any time.\r\n\r\n\r\nRemoving addition, using the right multiplier, and making sure LOP3 gets implemented are all more important for getting better speed and quality.\r\n\r\nLet me know when KLD eval is ready so we can triple verify this change actually provides 1-3% avg higher fidelity via lower MSE, lower perplexity, and lower KLD at all bitrates (especially lower ones). The speedup may grow to +10% too once lop3 is used.",
      "content_sha256": "af078abd18950174f31e420cfa711cdda0c02de4eaa9d6049da86ac28664b8f3",
      "created_at": "2025-05-03T14:39:23Z",
      "representation": "body",
      "revision_at": "2025-05-03T14:39:23Z",
      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6pywfE",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/pull/26#issuecomment-2848655300"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "louiehelm",
      "content": "Top 6 3INST MCG parameters found through exhaustive MSE sampling of all Vigna 32-bit multipliers (plotted with your visualization and RMS calculation):\r\n\r\n![0xE2A54B45](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c6db41b8-b91d-4e70-9a5b-5acff0de4da1)\r\n\r\n![0xFF7A83E5](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/39ad6da0-a690-4cc2-ad18-73a45a5fa234)\r\n\r\n![0xA2EC794D](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5ec2bcab-26ec-4787-8d6c-8f6cd8aad7cc)\r\n\r\n![0x00D0AA65](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dfc39b28-c58f-4a5e-a876-0a916006ad72)\r\n\r\n![0xCAF6A435](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ae5fbe6d-16b2-439f-a6c5-33943b54da39)\r\n\r\n![0xB26DB26D](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/833bddb8-e3e0-4a83-8bba-34b483a5a6a8)\r\n\r\n\r\nThese plots are a fine tool for getting a general feel for each codebook by examining part of its distribution. But do keep in mind that this is only plotting raw input <--> output for dim=1 for 8 different bitrates [1-bit - 8-bit]. However, the QTIP Trellis codes operate in 256 dimensions. So these charts are only showing 1 of the 256 distributions that effect overall performance. Also, unlike most applications where dim=1 is by far the most meaningful distribution, there's nothing special about dim=1 within a 256 dimension Trellis Coder. So it should be expected that quality of the 255 higher dimensions (aka higher-order spectral quality) actually matter equally in all dimensions for this application.\r\n\r\nJust pointing this out so we remember RMS=1.17 vs RMS=1.20 in these charts just means ~0.4% of all distributions are ~2.6% better. But that doesn't automatically mean the other 99.6% of the distribution quality will also be 2.6% better. Often higher order behavior is quite jagged and random and good distributions in one dimension only loosely correlate with distribution quality within other dimensions.\r\n\r\nThat's why I tested these six 3INST MCG values for actual MSE distortion using real 256 dimension Trellis Coding:\r\n\r\n![2-bit PLUS](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/95ea929f-b689-4abe-b8ec-35b3ee807003)\r\n\r\n![3-bit PLUS](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b522ccbe-1509-42fa-a51f-09cae88a82b9)\r\n\r\n![4-bit PLUS](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0b7445fb-0b28-463b-a499-c97bbe4eacce)\r\n\r\n\r\nY-axis re-scaled to distortion relative to an optimal codebook [2^(-2*bitrate)]\r\n\r\nAverage distortion and variance was plotted by sampling each decoder with 145-195 different 8192 [16 bit] Gaussian data chunks. from typing_extensions import override
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn
from ..models import Config
from . import Module
from ..ext import exllamav3_ext as ext

class RMSNorm(Module):

    def __init__(
        self,
        config: Config,
        key: str,
        rms_norm_eps: float,
        out_dtype: torch.dtype | None = None,
        qmap: str | None = None,
        constant_bias: float = 0.0
    ):
        super().__init__(config, key, None)
        assert qmap is None, "No quant scheme for RMSNorm"
        self.module_name = "RMSNorm"

        self.weight = None
        self.rms_norm_eps = rms_norm_eps
        self.out_dtype = out_dtype
        self._numel = None
        self.constant_bias = constant_bias

    @override
    def load(self, device: torch.device, **kwargs):
        self.device = device
        weight = self.config.stc.get_tensor(f"{self.key}.weight", self.device, float2half = True)
        self._numel = weight.numel()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(weight, requires_grad = False)

    @override
    def unload(self):
        self.device = None
        self.weight = None

    @override
    def get_tensors(self):
        return {
            f"{self.key}.weight": self.weight.data
        }

    def forward_torch(
        self,
        x: torch.Tensor,
        params: dict,
        out_dtype: torch.dtype | None = None,
    ) -> torch.Tensor:
        dtype = x.dtype
        x = x.float()
        var = x.pow(2).mean(dim = -1, keepdim = True) + self.rms_norm_eps
        x = x * torch.rsqrt(var)
        x = x.to(dtype)
        x = x * self.weight if self.constant_bias == 0.0 else x * (self.weight + self.constant_bias)
        x = x.to(out_dtype or self.out_dtype)
        return x

    @override
    def weights_numel(self):
        return self._numel

    @override
    def forward(
        self,
        x: torch.Tensor,
        params,
        out_dtype: torch.dtype | None = None,
    ) -> torch.Tensor:

        y = torch.empty_like(x, dtype = out_dtype or self.out_dtype)
        ext.rms_norm(x, self.weight, y, self.rms_norm_eps, self.constant_bias)
        return y", "encoding": "utf-8", "mode": "100644"}}
